problem: Real-world navigation data for wheeled robots usually requires platform-specific teleoperation, which is expensive and hard to scale. The cheaper human-collected data (worn rigs, web video) includes routes a wheeled robot cannot traverse, such as stairs, uncut curbs and narrow gaps. It also often lacks metric scale (e.g., CityWalker normalizes VO trajectories). Filtering these routes afterward cannot recover the wheeled-feasible alternatives that were never demonstrated.
motivation: UMI showed in manipulation that a cheap physical proxy can collect robot-free demonstrations that keep task-relevant constraints. The authors ask whether a rollator walker can do the same for wheeled navigation. A rollator cannot climb stairs, mount uncut curbs or fit through narrow gaps, so demonstrations are physically biased toward wheeled-feasible routes during collection. Public pedestrian collection also naturally keeps waiting and yielding behavior, which existing corpora rarely contain or explicitly filter out.
key_idea: Push an off-the-shelf rollator (~$250) carrying a LiDAR iPhone to collect human navigation demonstrations that are physically constrained to wheeled-feasible routes, then recover metric trajectories offline with Depth Anything 3 scale-anchored by the phone's LiDAR depth, and use them to fine-tune existing goal-conditioned visual navigation models (GNM/ViNT/NoMaD).
insight: The physical wheeled constraint plus retained low-motion data gives supervision that off-the-shelf robot-native checkpoints lack. In the closed-loop wheelchair tests, released ViNT drove toward uncut curbs and stairs (0/4 stops each), while UNI-fine-tuned ViNT stopped (3/4 and 4/4) and still traversed curb cuts (4/4). The stationary ablation isolates the pause data: removing low-motion windows (5.73% of training) raises stationary ADE by 68.0% versus removing the same number of random windows (0.336 vs 0.200 m), with little change in moving ADE. So the gain comes from pause demonstrations, not dataset size. LiDAR anchoring is essential for metric supervision: it cuts DA3 scale error from 7.67% to 3.14% on TUM and from 22.92% to 6.75% on KITTI. ORB-SLAM3 RGB-D tracks only partially on UNI (84.1% of frames, 10/30 complete recordings). Cross-corpus benefits are mixed: gains on SCAND/SiT, better heading on CODa, a regression on SACSoN.
method: Rollator-constrained collection: an operator pushes a commercial four-wheeled rollator with a phone mount and all four wheels on the ground. Routes must use curb cuts, ramps and lifts and avoid stairs, uncut curbs and narrow gaps. Adherence is audited via IMU stepping signatures and depth ground-plane step-height detection plus video review; no confirmed stair or uncut-curb traversals were found.

SensorVault iOS app (iPhone 16 Pro): records at 30 Hz 1280x720 JPEG RGB, 256x192 ARKit LiDAR depth plus confidence, and 6-DoF VIO. Also records 100 Hz IMU, GPS and audio on a shared monotonic clock, with intrinsics, fixed focus and MCAP storage. VIO is kept only for reference because 34.9% of VIO chunks showed implausible motion.

DA3+Anchor trajectory recovery: Depth Anything 3 runs on 48-frame windows at 4 Hz (~12 s) with 12-frame overlap and jointly predicts depth and camera poses up to scale. Windows are similarity-aligned on overlaps and chained, rejecting joins by RMS pose disagreement. One absolute scale per segment is the median over frames of the per-frame median ratio of LiDAR depth to predicted depth. Segments lacking metric support are rejected (8.3%).

Model-ready export: future poses are expressed relative to the current observation as metric waypoint targets paired with image goals. The snapshot has 1,087 trajectories and 117,512 frames at ~4 Hz; faces and plates are blurred with EgoBlur for release.

Policy adaptation: released GNM, ViNT and NoMaD checkpoints are fine-tuned (or trained from scratch) on UNI. Setup: up to 20 epochs, AdamW, lr 5e-4, cosine schedule with 4 warm-up epochs, batch size 128, 5 predicted waypoints.

Deployment on a powered wheelchair: iPhone at 0.80 m (vs 0.40 m during collection) streams RGB to a laptop (RTX 3070 Ti) for inference. Waypoints are converted to linear/angular Twist commands for the wheelchair's Jetson Nano, with a 0.30 m/s speed cap and an operator dead-man enable button.

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark (R2R/ObjectNav etc.) is used. Most results are open-loop waypoint-prediction errors (ADE/FDE in m, direction error in degrees) on UNI held-out data and external corpora, plus a small real-wheelchair closed-loop test reported as success counts. The split sizes for the external-corpus evaluations (SACSoN, SCAND, CODa) are not specified. Stationary-ablation variants (random removal: moving 0.288 / stationary 0.200; stationary removal: 0.295 / 0.336) are omitted from the entries but noted in the insight. The figures referenced in the text contain no image content in the source.
results: On held-out UNI outings, fine-tuning on UNI reduces ADE by 17.4–24.8% relative to released checkpoints: GNM 0.318→0.239, ViNT 0.322→0.245, NoMaD 0.321→0.265 m. Each fine-tuned model also beats its from-scratch counterpart, and ViNT's stationary ADE drops 65.7% (0.435→0.149 m). External-corpus results are mixed. UNI-ViNT improves all metrics on SCAND and SiT, reduces directional error on CODa by 25.9% (6.65→4.93°) while slightly worsening ADE/FDE, and regresses on SACSoN. Against EgoWalk at matched distance it gets 36.4% lower heading error on CODa (3.89 vs 6.12°), but numerically worse shape-ADE/FDE. On a powered wheelchair, UNI-ViNT stops before uncut curbs in 3/4 and staircases in 4/4 trials versus 0/4 for released ViNT, and both complete 4/4 curb-cut traversals.
limitations: Closed-loop evidence is very small: one trial at each of 4 locations per scenario on a single wheelchair, with one uncut-curb failure. Most evaluation is open-loop waypoint error rather than navigation success.

Cross-dataset gains depend on corpus and metric (regression on SACSoN, worse ADE/FDE on CODa), so fine-tuning can erode previously learned domains. The authors suggest joint training with robot-native data.

The rollator only approximates wheeled feasibility; transfer depends on the target robot's footprint, ground clearance and slope limits. Predicting low motion does not show that the model understands why to stop or when to resume, and no annotations of signal state or pedestrian interactions exist yet.
